blocks.title: Therapeutic communication
blocks.learner_title: How you get a history at all

cold_open.text: Two crews, the same patient, twenty minutes apart. The first gets "chest pain, started tonight, that is all he will say". The second gets a two-week history, a medication he stopped taking, and the sentence that changes the whole call. Nobody administered anything in between.
cold_open.decision_point: What did the second crew do differently?

screens.body_md:
**The history is most of your assessment**, and it only exists if the patient tells you. Everything downstream — impression, treatment, destination — rests on a conversation.

That is the reason communication is treated as a clinical skill here rather than as manner. A frightened patient hands you less, and you then decide with less.

**Open first, closed after.** "Tell me what happened today" gets you a story. "Are you having chest pain?" gets you your own hypothesis back, confirmed.

Closed questions are for filling the gaps once the account exists. Asked first, they end the narrative before it starts, and you never hear the part you would not have asked about.

The cost of the open question is about twenty seconds. The cost of skipping it is everything the patient was going to volunteer.

**Leading questions manufacture findings.** Ask "is the pain crushing?" and you will get crushing pain, which you then chart, hand over, and treat as an observation.

You cannot later tell your own suggestion apart from the patient’s symptom. That is why this is a reliability problem rather than a matter of style.

**Four habits do most of the work.** Get to eye level. Allow silence — people fill it, often with the important part. Reflect back in their words. And do not finish their sentences, because you finish them with your own idea.

All four cost seconds. Together they change the quality of everything you write afterwards.

None of them is a personality trait. They are techniques, and they work for people who do not find this easy.

**Keep their words.** A patient who says something feels "wrong" has told you something; ask what they mean and record the phrase as well as your reading of it.

"Uncooperative" in a chart is nearly always a description of a conversation that was handled badly. The fix is posture, pace, and saying what happens next.

blocks.callback_md:
They sat down, asked one open question, and then said nothing for long enough to be uncomfortable.

The first crew asked a list. The second asked "tell me what happened" and let the silence run. **The two weeks, the stopped medication and the sentence that mattered were all available to both crews** — one of them made a room in which they could be said.

blocks.title: Barriers
blocks.learner_title: When the usual way does not work

cold_open.text: She speaks Vietnamese and a few words of English. Her granddaughter is eleven and is translating, and crying. You have pale, sweaty, a pulse of 118, and "something hurts". The hospital is twenty minutes away and you have no history at all.

screens.body_md:
**A barrier removes most of your assessment**, which is why it is a patient safety issue rather than an inconvenience. Strip out the history and you are judging a stranger from across the room.

That is the argument for spending the extra minutes: they buy back the part of the assessment that matters most.

**Family interpreters get used because they are fast**, and they carry two costs. Clinically significant errors are more frequent, and the patient may leave things out in front of their own family.

The second is invisible to you. Use family when nothing else is available and the need is immediate, then get professional interpretation and note in the chart who interpreted.

**Hearing loss: face them, quieten the room, speak clearly at a normal volume.** Shouting distorts the sounds and reads as aggression.

Write it down if that is faster, and use their own hearing aid if it is within reach. Talking to the relative instead removes the patient from their own assessment, which is where the information is.

**Cognitive impairment: one short question at a time, with time to answer it.** Most patients with dementia can answer something, and slowing down recovers more than people expect.

With children, get to their eye level, keep a trusted adult close, and warn before you touch. Never promise it will not hurt — if it does, you have spent the only trust you had.

**Expression of pain varies enormously**, between individuals and between cultures. Reading stoicism as mild pain is a documented source of undertreatment.

And the record should show the barrier, what you did about it, and who interpreted. A history taken through a frightened child is a different piece of evidence, and the next reader should be able to tell.

blocks.callback_md:
A telephone interpreter, requested en route. Three minutes, and "something hurts" becomes upper abdominal pain since yesterday morning, after eating, constant, with two episodes of vomiting overnight.

**Nothing else on that call would have produced that**, and the granddaughter was never going to — partly because of what an eleven-year-old can translate, and partly because her grandmother was not going to say it in front of her.

blocks.title: Radio and dispatch

cold_open.text: You key the microphone with no plan and talk for fifty seconds. At the other end a nurse who is holding a pen writes down three of the nine things you said, in the wrong order, and misses the one you were actually calling about.
cold_open.decision_point: Which part of that was the radio’s fault?

screens.body_md:
**The receiver is writing while listening, and cannot ask you to go back.** One pass, no replay.

That single fact drives everything else: plan before you key, pause briefly after keying so the first syllable is not clipped, speak at a normal volume and pace, and keep it short and in a predictable order.

Everything that goes wrong on a radio goes wrong because somebody forgot that the person listening cannot rewind.

**The order is boring on purpose.** Who is calling and when you arrive. Age, sex, chief complaint. Pertinent history and findings. Treatment and response. What you are asking them to have ready.

Same shape every time, and the person at the other end can prepare the next field instead of searching for it.

Varying it to sound less mechanical costs the receiver more than it gains you.

**Plain language, not codes.** The same code means different things two counties apart, and a multi-agency incident needs everyone to mean the same thing.

Common terminology is a core principle of incident management for that reason. On a large scene, code confusion is not a nuisance — it is people acting on different information.

**Read back every order.** Drug, dose, route, repeated and confirmed before you give anything.

Four seconds, on a noisy channel, and it is the only step in the chain that catches a misheard dose. Chapter 1 said this already; it is worth saying twice, because it is skipped under exactly the conditions that produce the error.

**Anyone with a scanner is listening.** Clinical detail is necessary; the patient’s name almost never is, and it is the part that identifies the person.

Dispatch information is a hypothesis from a frightened third party. Reassess from what you find, tell dispatch when it differs, and chart both.

blocks.callback_md:
None of it. The radio worked perfectly.

Fifty seconds of unplanned speech, delivered once, to somebody writing by hand — three items out of nine is about what that gets you. **Plan it, put it in the same order every time, and put the ask at the end where it is remembered.** The nurse is not the bottleneck; the structure is.

blocks.title: Crew, family and other agencies

cold_open.text: Your partner has drawn up a dose that looks wrong to you. They are experienced, you are three months in, the patient is unwell, and there are four other people in the room. You have about six seconds.

screens.body_md:
**Hints are not heard under load.** Attention narrows, and inference is the first thing to go — the same perceptual narrowing Chapter 2 described.

"Are you sure about that?" relies on the other person having spare attention, which at that moment is exactly what nobody has.

Aviation worked this out decades ago, and the finding transferred to medicine unchanged: indirect challenges fail when they are needed most.

**A challenge that works has four features.** It names the specific concern. It comes before the action. It addresses the action rather than the person. And it is repeated once, more directly, if it is not addressed.

"Stop — that is 10 milligrams, the order was 1." Six words, and every one of them is doing work.

**A frightened relative with a job is a help.** Fetch the medications. Hold the door. Tell me the timeline in a minute.

The same person with nothing to do talks over your assessment, because being ignored while someone you love is ill is intolerable. Redirect rather than remove: you lose a source and their trust when you send them out.

And they will tell the hospital, and everyone else, how the crew behaved in that room.

**Do not offer a diagnosis you do not have.** It gets repeated to everyone, including the hospital, as a fact.

Say what you are doing and what you are looking for. "I am checking his rhythm and his sugar, and we are going to the hospital" is true, settles a room, and creates no expectation you cannot meet.

**Command and clinical authority are different things.** Incident command owns the scene, access and safety. The highest-level clinician caring for the patient owns the clinical decisions.

Confusing the two is a recurring source of conflict on multi-agency scenes. Disagreements that are not about immediate safety move away from the patient.

blocks.callback_md:
"Stop. That looks like 10 milligrams — the order was 1."

Specific, before the act, about the syringe rather than about them, and loud enough for the room. If it is waved off, say it once more and more directly. **Three months in is irrelevant** — the dose is either right or it is not, and the only version of this that ends badly is the one where you hinted.

blocks.title: Handover
blocks.learner_title: Ninety seconds that have to work

cold_open.text: You have forty minutes of assessment, treatment and response to transfer, to someone who is typing, in a corridor, in about ninety seconds. Whatever does not survive that transfer is gone, and the patient is about to belong to them.

screens.body_md:
**Handover is a recognised point of failure**, because responsibility and information move at the same moment and only one of them is guaranteed to arrive.

What the evidence supports is structure: structured handover reduces information loss. What it does not support is any particular acronym being better than the others.

The evidence base is mostly low quality, and it points consistently in that one direction.

**So use your service’s structure, every time.** Most of the benefit comes from consistency — the receiving team learns what is coming and stops having to search for it.

Which named format your service uses is a local decision. What every one of them is a mnemonic for is the same short list.

**Who the patient is.** Age, sex, presenting problem, in one sentence.
**What happened**, including onset or mechanism, and the timing — time is what is most often lost.
**What you found**, including the relevant negatives.
**What you did, and what it did.**
**What you are handing over** — the ask goes last, where it is remembered.

**Relevant negatives are part of the findings**, not padding. Without them the next clinician cannot tell a finding that is absent from one nobody looked for.

And keep judgements out. "Frequent flyer, probably nothing" follows the patient through the department and changes how they are treated, on no evidence at all.

**A handover nobody received has not happened.** If the person taking your patient is typing and not listening, stop and ask for ninety seconds.

It feels awkward once. Continuing feels fine and transfers nothing, and the information you lose is the information nobody else has.

Asking for ninety seconds is not rude. Handing over to the back of someone’s head is.

blocks.callback_md:
Who she is. What happened and when. What you found, negatives included. What you did and whether it worked. And what you need from them.

That is the list every named structure encodes, and **it survives ninety seconds if you say it in the same order every time.** What will not survive is the forty-minute chronology, and what should not survive is your opinion of the patient.

*Which structure this service uses belongs in the local layer. It has not been set here.*

blocks.title: What the report is for

cold_open.text: You write the report at 0450, after the fourth call of the night, for nobody in particular. Over the next two years it is read by a physician, a quality reviewer, a billing coder and — on one of these, though you will not know which — a lawyer.
cold_open.decision_point: Which of them were you writing for?

screens.body_md:
**Four audiences, one document.** Clinicians continuing care. Quality review looking across many calls. Billing. And occasionally litigation.

Writing for one is how a report ends up unusable for the other three. A specific, objective clinical narrative happens to serve all four, which is why that is the standard.

None of the four wants your opinion of the patient. All four want to know what you found and what you did about it.

**The structured fields are not busywork.** Patterns across many calls can only be found in comparable fields; narrative cannot be aggregated.

The national dataset is built from them, and it is what the continuous quality improvement of Chapter 1 actually runs on. Your narrative serves the next clinician; the fields serve the next thousand patients.

**Times have to be true.** They are used for system review, and adjusted times are a quiet and common form of falsification.

They also corrupt the aggregate, which defeats the point of collecting them. A time that makes the service look better is a time that makes the data useless.

**Write it while you can still see the room.** Nothing degrades a report like three more calls; by the end of a shift several of them have blurred together.

And care you gave but did not record is treated as not having happened. Said in Chapter 3 already, and it is the sentence that changes how people write.

Ten minutes at the time is worth an hour of trying to remember, and the ten minutes produce something true.

**The no-transport call gets a full report.** What you assessed, what you found, what was discussed, and the disposition.

These are the calls most likely to be read closely afterwards and the ones where records are thinnest — the same inverse relationship Chapter 3 described about refusals, and for the same reason.

blocks.callback_md:
All four, whether you meant to or not.

The physician needs what you found and what it did. Quality review needs the times and the fields. Billing needs the disposition. And the lawyer — on the one call you could not have predicted — needs to know what was assessed, at what time, and why you decided what you decided.

**A specific, objective narrative written while you can still see the room serves all of them.** Nothing else does.

blocks.title: Writing the narrative

cold_open.text: Two entries about the same patient. One says "patient was drunk and belligerent". The other says "odour of alcohol on breath, unsteady on standing, speech slurred, declined the oxygen mask stating it made him feel trapped". Both took about the same time to type.

screens.body_md:
**Objective means observed, measured, or quoted.** Subjective means concluded.

The distinction is practical rather than philosophical: an observation can be checked by somebody else, and a characterisation cannot. "Drunk" is a conclusion. Three observations underneath it are evidence.

And the observations survive being read out loud by a stranger. The conclusion does not.

**Quote the patient.** Their own words carry clinical information that a paraphrase loses, and they cannot be argued with afterwards.

Quote three things in particular: how they described the symptom, anything they said in refusing, and anything you are relying on. "It feels like an elephant on my chest" is a finding.

**Specific beats impressive.** "Large amount of bleeding" means whatever the reader decides. "Approximately 300 mL, soaked through two trauma dressings" means something.

"Patient improved" is nothing. "After 4 mg, pain fell from 9/10 to 4/10 over six minutes" is a measurement, a time and a response.

Neither of the specific versions took longer to type than the vague one it replaced.

**Labels do three kinds of damage at once.** "Non-compliant" is unverifiable, it prejudices every clinician who reads it next, and it replaces the observation that would have been useful.

Write what happened instead. Then the next person can try something, rather than inheriting a verdict.

"Declined the oxygen mask, stated it made him feel trapped" is four seconds longer to type and it is actionable.

**Record the reasoning where reasoning was needed** — a departure from protocol most of all. Chapter 3 said conduct is judged against a reasonable provider in the same circumstances; your reasoning is the evidence of what you were doing.

And use the same structure every time. It is what protects you from your own fatigue at 0450.

blocks.callback_md:
The second one still means something in two years, to someone who was not there.

The first is a verdict. It cannot be checked, it tells the next clinician how to feel about the patient before they have met him, and it has thrown away the three observations that would have been useful — **including the reason he refused the mask**, which is the only line in either entry that somebody could have acted on.

blocks.title: Errors, corrections and falsification

cold_open.text: An hour after you submitted the report you realise a figure is wrong. The system will let you open it and change it, and nobody would ever ask. It would take four seconds and the record would look clean.
cold_open.decision_point: Why is that the worst available option?

screens.body_md:
**Everyone makes charting errors.** What the system cannot work with is a record it cannot trust — which is why the response to the error matters more than the error.

A correction shows four things: the original entry, the corrected information, when the change was made, and who made it. Nothing is erased.

That is not a concession to bureaucracy. It is what lets somebody reading the chart tell a correction apart from a rewrite.

**Late entries are normal.** An assessment you performed and forgot to record goes in as a clearly marked late entry, with today’s date and time.

Unmarked ones are not normal. The difference between the two is a single line of text, and it is the difference between record keeping and altering a record.

**Falsification is recording what did not happen, or altering the record to conceal what did.** A vital sign you did not take. A time adjusted to fit a target. An entry quietly deleted.

All three are the same act. Intent to misrepresent is the line, and it is nothing to do with how small the change was.

**Concealing converts a survivable mistake into dishonesty**, and once one entry is shown to have been altered, every other entry you have written is read differently.

This is Chapter 2 on near misses in a different setting. The organisation absorbs errors easily. It cannot absorb a record nobody can rely on.

Which is why the open correction is the self-interested choice as well as the honest one.

**Electronic systems log every change**, with a timestamp and a user, whether or not it is visible in the document — and the trail can be produced in litigation.

People are regularly surprised by this. It is the practical argument for openness: the trail exists either way, and only one version of you looks reasonable in it.

blocks.callback_md:
Because the system logged it, and you have just turned a wrong number into an altered record.

The error was survivable and unremarkable. The quiet edit is neither. **Add a correction that shows the original, the change, the time and your name** — it takes a minute rather than four seconds, and it is the only version that still looks like a mistake afterwards rather than like a decision.

blocks.title: Refusals, restraint and mass casualty
blocks.learner_title: The records most likely to be read

cold_open.text: Three calls that end without a hospital bed to absorb them: a refusal, a restrained patient, and twenty people at a crash site. Each produces the thinnest record of your week, and each is far more likely than the others to be read closely by someone you have never met.
cold_open.decision_point: Why does it work out that way round?

screens.body_md:
**The refusal record is the highest-risk document you write.** Four things: the capacity assessment as a conversation, the specific risks you named, that the patient repeated them back, and the plan agreed.

None of those is the signature. Chapter 3 covered the decision; this is what has to survive it on paper.

If a reader cannot tell from your note what the patient understood, the refusal is undocumented however many boxes were ticked.

**Restraint is a high-risk intervention and is documented like one.** Why it was necessary, what was tried first, what was used, the time applied, and repeated checks of circulation and respiration.

Restraint-associated deaths share a recurring feature: inadequate monitoring. The record is where monitoring is demonstrated, or where its absence is.

**A no-transport is still a patient contact.** Assessment performed including vital signs, what was discussed and advised, the disposition and who the patient was left with, and that they were told they could call again.

"No treatment required" documents a conclusion and none of the assessment behind it.

**Mass casualty documentation is a tracking record first.** Identify each patient, record the triage category, and record where each one went and with whom.

Twenty full narratives written on scene would mean nobody knows where patient fourteen is. Track first; the full report follows afterwards.

The question the record has to answer that night is where everybody went, and it has to answer it for all of them.

**Suspected abuse: findings and quotations, not conclusions.** Describe the bruising, its pattern and distribution, quote what was said and by whom, and record that a report was made to the agency your state requires.

Investigation belongs to somebody else. Observation belongs to you, and it is what makes the report worth anything.

blocks.callback_md:
Because there is no hospital record downstream to fill the gap. On a transported patient, everything you missed gets picked up by the department and written down by somebody else. On these three, your report is the entire account of what happened.

**Scrutiny and thin records arrive together**, and always in that order — which is exactly the wrong way round, and entirely fixable in the ten minutes after the call.

blocks.title: Integration — doorway to chart
blocks.learner_title: Carrying one story all the way

cold_open.text: One patient’s story has to travel from a doorway, through a barrier, over a radio, across a corridor handover, into a chart that somebody reads two years later. Every one of those is a place it can be dropped, and most of them are places nobody would notice it had been.
cold_open.decision_point: Where does it actually get lost?

screens.body_md:
**Four transfers, and the story has to survive all of them.**

Patient to you, through whatever barrier is in the way. You to the hospital over the radio, in one pass. You to the receiving team, in ninety seconds, in a corridor. And you to the record, at the end of the shift, for four readers you will never meet.

What follows is one call. It nearly goes wrong at three of the four.

blocks.callback_md:
At the first transfer, and nowhere else — because it was fixed there.

An eleven-year-old was carrying a history she could not carry, and her grandmother would not have given it to her anyway. One telephone call turned an appearance into an assessment, and everything downstream — the radio request, the handover, the narrative, the two-day delay finally explained — came from those three minutes.

**The rest of the chapter is about not dropping what you were given. This part is about getting it at all.**

items.stem: What does active listening involve?

options.text: Attending, allowing silence, and reflecting back to confirm you understood
options.rationale: It is an observable set of behaviours, not an attitude.

options.text: Nodding while planning your next question
options.rationale: That is the thing active listening is contrasted with.

options.text: Writing everything down verbatim as they speak
options.rationale: Recording is not the same as listening, and it can block it.

options.text: Repeating the question until they answer it properly
options.rationale: That is interrogation.

items.stem: A patient uses a word you are not sure about — they say they feel "wrong". What do you do with it?

options.text: Ask what they mean by it, and record their word as well as your interpretation
options.rationale: The patient’s own word is data, and "a sense of doom" has clinical weight.

options.text: Translate it into a symptom you recognise and chart that
options.rationale: You have replaced their account with your guess and lost the original.

options.text: Ignore it as non-specific
options.rationale: Non-specific is not the same as unimportant.

options.text: Record it as anxiety
options.rationale: That is a diagnosis, and it is not yours to make from one word.
