options.rationale: He probably does. That is not the problem.

options.text: There is no concern if the patient agrees
options.rationale: Agreement does not remove either problem.

items.explanation_md: Use it when nothing else is available and the need is immediate, and get professional interpretation as soon as you can. Note in the chart who interpreted.
items.source_ref: Flores G. The impact of medical interpreter services on the quality of health care: a systematic review. Med Care Res Rev 2005;62:255–99.

items.stem: Select what helps when communicating with a patient who is hard of hearing.

options.text: Face them directly so they can see your mouth
options.rationale: Many people lip-read more than they realise.

options.text: Reduce background noise where you can
options.rationale: Turn the radio down; move away from the engine.

options.text: Speak clearly at a normal pace rather than louder
options.rationale: Shouting distorts the sounds and looks aggressive.

options.text: Write it down, or use their own hearing aid if they have one
options.rationale: Both are often the fastest route to being understood.

options.text: Speak to the relative instead so the conversation moves
options.rationale: It cuts the patient out of their own assessment.

items.explanation_md: Face, quiet, clear, and write it if needed. Shouting at someone with hearing loss makes them harder to understand, not easier.
items.source_ref: Americans with Disabilities Act, 28 CFR 35.160 — effective communication and auxiliary aids.

items.stem: How should you talk to a patient with dementia who cannot follow a long question?

options.text: One short question at a time, allow extra time, and use their name
options.rationale: Short, single-idea questions with time to answer them.

options.text: Ask the questions faster so they do not lose track
options.rationale: Speed worsens it.

options.text: Direct all questions to the caregiver
options.rationale: Use the caregiver to corroborate, not to replace the patient.

options.text: Raise your voice
options.rationale: Volume does not address a comprehension problem.

items.explanation_md: Most patients with dementia can answer something. Slowing down and shortening the question usually recovers more than you expect.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Does this help across a language or cultural barrier?

rows.label: Using a professional interpreter service where one is reachable
Speaking louder in English
Asking permission before touching, and explaining each step
Assuming a quiet patient is not in much pain

items.explanation_md: Expression of pain varies enormously between people and between cultures. Stoicism is not a vital sign, and reading it as one is a documented source of undertreatment.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What is the most useful approach with a frightened five-year-old?

options.text: Get to their eye level, keep a trusted adult close, and explain in short concrete words before you touch them
options.rationale: Position, a familiar adult, and warning before contact.

options.text: Work quickly and explain afterwards
options.rationale: Surprise increases distress and makes the rest of the assessment harder.

options.text: Tell them it will not hurt
options.rationale: If it does, you have spent the only trust you had.

options.text: Separate them from the parent so they concentrate
options.rationale: That removes the one thing making the situation tolerable.

items.explanation_md: Never promise it will not hurt. "This will pinch for a second and then it is done" is both true and easier to hear.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Why does a communication barrier become a patient safety issue rather than an inconvenience?

options.text: Because the history is where most of your information comes from, so a barrier removes most of your assessment
options.rationale: You end up deciding on vital signs and appearance alone.

options.text: Because it lengthens on-scene time
options.rationale: It does, and that is not the safety issue.

options.text: Because documentation becomes harder
options.rationale: A consequence, not the mechanism.

options.text: Because it frustrates the crew
options.rationale: Not a patient safety mechanism.

items.explanation_md: Strip out the history and you are left assessing a stranger from across the room. That is why the workaround is worth the extra minutes it costs.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Sort each adjustment to the barrier it addresses.

options.text: Face the patient, reduce background noise, write it down
options.rationale: Hearing loss.

options.text: Professional interpretation, and note who interpreted
options.rationale: A language barrier.

options.text: One short question at a time, with extra time to answer
options.rationale: Cognitive impairment.

options.text: Use the patient’s own hearing aid if they have it with them
options.rationale: Hearing, and it is regularly overlooked.

items.explanation_md: Each barrier has a specific adjustment. Louder and faster addresses none of them, and it is what most people reach for first.
items.source_ref: Americans with Disabilities Act, 28 CFR 35.160 — effective communication and auxiliary aids.

items.stem: What should the record show when communication was difficult?

options.text: What the barrier was, what you did about it, and who interpreted if anyone did
options.rationale: It explains a thin history without making it look like inattention.

options.text: That the patient was uncooperative
options.rationale: It attributes to the patient what was a barrier.

options.text: Nothing — it is not clinical information
options.rationale: It is exactly the context the next reader needs.

options.text: Only the final answers you obtained
options.rationale: Then nobody can judge how reliable they are.

items.explanation_md: A history obtained through a frightened ten-year-old interpreter is a different piece of evidence from one taken directly, and the chart should let the reader tell which they have.
items.source_ref: Flores G. The impact of medical interpreter services on the quality of health care: a systematic review. Med Care Res Rev 2005;62:255–99.

items.stem: Why is plain language preferred over agency codes on multi-agency incidents?

options.text: Codes differ between agencies, and an incident with several agencies needs everyone to mean the same thing
options.rationale: Common terminology is a core principle of incident management for exactly this reason.

options.text: Codes take longer to say
options.rationale: They are usually shorter, which is why they persisted.

options.text: Codes are prohibited by federal law
options.rationale: They are not prohibited; plain language is recommended for interoperability.

options.text: Plain language is more polite
options.rationale: Not the reason.

items.explanation_md: The same code means different things two counties apart. On a large incident that is not a nuisance — it is people acting on different information.
items.source_ref: FEMA National Incident Management System — common terminology and plain language.

items.stem: Medical control gives you a drug order over the radio and the channel is noisy. What do you do before giving it?

options.text: Repeat the order back in full — drug, dose, route — and have it confirmed
options.rationale: The read-back is the only step in the chain that catches a misheard dose.

options.text: Give it, since the order was clear enough
options.rationale: "Clear enough" on a noisy channel is how doses get misheard.

options.text: Ask your partner what they heard
options.rationale: Useful, and it is not confirmation from the person who gave the order.

options.text: Write it down and give it
options.rationale: Writing down what you misheard does not correct it.

items.explanation_md: Four seconds, and it catches the error at the only moment it can still be caught. Chapter 1 said this; it is worth saying twice.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Select what makes a radio transmission effective.

options.text: Plan what you will say before keying the microphone
options.rationale: Thinking on air occupies a channel other people need.

options.text: Key, pause briefly, then speak — the first syllable is often clipped
options.rationale: A short pause after keying stops the first word disappearing.

options.text: Speak at a normal conversational volume and pace
options.rationale: Shouting distorts; rushing loses words.

options.text: Keep it brief and structured, in a predictable order
options.rationale: The receiver knows what is coming and can write it down.

options.text: Include the patient’s name so the hospital can look them up
options.rationale: Names are not broadcast; it is an unnecessary disclosure over an open channel.

items.explanation_md: Plan, pause, speak normally, keep it short and in the same order every time. The last one is what lets a busy nurse write while you talk.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Put a radio report to the receiving hospital into a workable order.

options.text: Unit identification and estimated time of arrival
options.rationale: Who is calling and when you will arrive, so they can plan.

options.text: Patient age, sex and chief complaint
options.rationale: The headline, in one line.

options.text: Pertinent history and assessment findings
options.rationale: Enough to size the problem, not the whole chart.

options.text: Treatment given and the response to it
options.rationale: What has already been done, and whether it worked.

options.text: What you are requesting from them
options.rationale: The ask goes last, where it is remembered.

items.explanation_md: Who and when, who the patient is, what you found, what you did, what you need. Every service words it differently and the shape is the same.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What should not go out over an open radio channel?

options.text: The patient’s name and other identifying detail that the receiving team does not need en route
options.rationale: Broadcast channels are not private, and the name adds nothing clinically.

options.text: The chief complaint
options.rationale: It is the point of the call.

options.text: Vital signs
options.rationale: Clinically necessary.

options.text: Your estimated time of arrival
options.rationale: Needed for them to prepare.

items.explanation_md: Anyone with a scanner is listening. Clinical information is necessary; the name almost never is, and it is the part that identifies the person.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Belongs in the radio report, or wait for the bedside handover?

rows.label: Age, sex, chief complaint and estimated arrival time
The full medication list from the kitchen drawer
A request for a specialty team to be waiting
The patient’s exact words about their symptoms

items.explanation_md: The radio buys preparation: what is coming, when, and what you need ready. Detail that cannot be acted on before you arrive belongs at the bedside.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Why does a predictable order matter more on the radio than in conversation?

options.text: The receiver is writing while listening, and a known order lets them prepare the next field
options.rationale: Structure is what makes a one-pass verbal message usable.

options.text: It sounds more professional
options.rationale: It does, and that is not the reason.

options.text: It is shorter
options.rationale: Not necessarily shorter — just easier to receive.

options.text: It is required by the licence
options.rationale: Not a licensing requirement.

items.explanation_md: Nobody can ask you to go back. One pass, no replay, and someone writing it down — which is why the order is worth being boring about.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Dispatch gives you information that turns out to be wrong on arrival. What follows?

options.text: Reassess from what you find, and tell dispatch so the record and any responding resources are corrected
options.rationale: Dispatch information is a starting point, and the correction matters to whoever comes next.

options.text: Treat the dispatch information as authoritative
options.rationale: It comes from a caller who may be frightened, remote or mistaken.

options.text: Say nothing, to avoid criticising the dispatcher
options.rationale: The correction is about resources and the record, not about blame.

options.text: Document the dispatch information only
options.rationale: The chart should show what you actually found.

items.explanation_md: Dispatch is a hypothesis from a third party. Chart what was dispatched and what you found, particularly when they differ.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: You believe your partner is about to give the wrong drug. What is the effective thing to say?

options.text: Say it plainly and specifically — name the drug and the concern — and say it before the act, not after
options.rationale: Specific, direct, and in time to change anything.

options.text: Hint at it so they can save face
options.rationale: Hints are routinely missed under pressure, and this is where that gets someone hurt.

options.text: Wait and raise it after the call
options.rationale: Afterwards is too late for the only moment that mattered.

options.text: Take the syringe from them
options.rationale: It may end in a struggle, and speaking is faster.

items.explanation_md: Indirect challenge under pressure has a long history of not being heard, across aviation and medicine alike. Name the drug, name the concern, out loud.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: A family member is talking over your assessment and will not stop. What works best?

options.text: Give them a specific job that helps, and tell them you will come to their account next
options.rationale: Redirects the energy and keeps them inside the process.

options.text: Ask them to leave the room
options.rationale: Sometimes necessary, and it costs you a source and often their trust.

options.text: Ignore them and continue
options.rationale: They will escalate, because they are frightened and not being heard.

options.text: Ask them to write it down while you work
options.rationale: Better than ignoring, and still a way of getting rid of them.

items.explanation_md: Fetch the medications. Hold the door. Tell me the timeline in a minute. A frightened relative with a task is a help, and the same person with nothing to do is an obstacle.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Select what makes a crew challenge more likely to be heard.

options.text: Naming the specific concern rather than hinting
options.rationale: Specificity is what makes it actionable.

options.text: Saying it before the action, not after
options.rationale: A challenge after the fact is a debrief.

options.text: Addressing the action rather than the person
options.rationale: "That dose looks high" lands better than "you are wrong".

options.text: Escalating once if the concern is not addressed
options.rationale: One repeat, more directly, is the recognised pattern.

options.text: Raising it later in front of the receiving team
options.rationale: It humiliates without fixing anything, and it stops the next challenge coming.

items.explanation_md: Specific, early, about the action, and repeated once if it is not heard. That is a challenge; everything else is a comment.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Likely to be heard under pressure, or not?

rows.label: "Stop — that is 10 milligrams, the order was 1."
"Are you sure about that?"
"I am not comfortable with this dose, can we check it together?"
A raised eyebrow across the patient

items.explanation_md: The two that work name something specific. The two that fail rely on the other person having spare attention, which under pressure is the thing nobody has.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: On a scene with fire and law enforcement, who should be giving the clinical direction?

options.text: The highest-level clinician caring for the patient, working within the incident command structure
options.rationale: Clinical care and scene command are different authorities, and both exist at once.

options.text: Whichever agency arrived first
options.rationale: Arrival order does not confer clinical authority.

options.text: The law enforcement officer in charge of the scene
options.rationale: They command the scene; they do not direct patient care.

options.text: Whoever has the most years of service
options.rationale: Seniority is not the same as clinical level.

items.explanation_md: Scene safety and access sit with incident command. Clinical decisions sit with the clinician. Confusing the two is a recurring source of conflict on multi-agency scenes.
items.source_ref: FEMA National Incident Management System — common terminology and plain language.

items.stem: Why is a hint a poor way to raise a safety concern on a busy scene?

options.text: Under high workload people hear the literal words and miss the implication, so the concern never lands
options.rationale: Attention narrows, and inference is the first thing to go.

options.text: It is unprofessional
options.rationale: It is not primarily an etiquette question.

options.text: It takes longer
options.rationale: It is usually shorter, which is part of the appeal.

options.text: It embarrasses the other person
options.rationale: It is designed not to, and that is the trade being made.

items.explanation_md: The same perceptual narrowing from Chapter 2 shows up here. You cannot rely on somebody inferring anything at the moment they are most loaded.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What is the best way to handle a disagreement with another crew in front of the patient?

options.text: Move it away from the patient if it is not about immediate safety, and say so plainly
options.rationale: A patient watching their clinicians argue loses confidence in both.

options.text: Settle it there so the patient knows you are thorough
options.rationale: They do not read it that way.

options.text: Defer entirely to avoid conflict
options.rationale: Deferring on a safety issue is not conflict avoidance, it is a decision.

options.text: Continue and raise it at the hospital
options.rationale: Too late if it affects what happens now.

items.explanation_md: Immediate safety is said out loud, immediately, wherever you are. Everything else moves two metres away.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: A relative asks what is wrong with the patient while you are still assessing. What do you say?

options.text: What you are doing and what you are looking for, without offering a diagnosis you do not have
options.rationale: Honest, informative, and it does not create an expectation you cannot meet.

options.text: Your best guess at the diagnosis
options.rationale: It gets repeated to everyone, including the hospital, as a fact.

options.text: That you cannot discuss it
options.rationale: Unhelpful and usually untrue.

options.text: That everything will be fine
options.rationale: You do not know that, and if it is not, that sentence is remembered.

items.explanation_md: "I am checking his heart rhythm and his sugar, and we are going to the hospital" is truthful and settles a room. A guess repeated as a diagnosis does the opposite.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What does the evidence actually support about structured handover tools?

options.text: Structure reduces information loss; evidence that any one named tool beats another is weak
options.rationale: The benefit attaches to having a structure, not to a particular acronym.

options.text: One specific tool has been shown superior to all others
options.rationale: No tool has good evidence of superiority over the alternatives.

options.text: Structure makes no measurable difference
options.rationale: Information loss is reduced by structured handover.

options.text: Handover quality cannot be studied
options.rationale: It has been studied, mostly at low quality, and consistently in one direction.

items.explanation_md: So: use your service’s structure and use it every time. Arguing about which acronym is better is a distraction from the finding that actually holds.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Select what any adequate handover has to carry, whatever the format is called.

options.text: Who the patient is — age, sex and the presenting problem
options.rationale: The headline the receiving team builds everything else onto.

options.text: What happened, including mechanism or onset and timing
options.rationale: Time is what is most often lost at handover.

options.text: What you found, including the relevant negatives
options.rationale: What is absent shapes the differential as much as what is present.

options.text: What you did and how the patient responded
options.rationale: Response to treatment is information nobody else has.

options.text: Your impression of whether the patient was exaggerating
options.rationale: An opinion that prejudices the next assessment.

items.explanation_md: Who, what happened, what you found, what you did and what it did. Every structure in use is a mnemonic for that list.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Put a bedside handover into an order the receiving team can follow.

options.text: Identification: age, sex and chief complaint
options.rationale: Who this is, in one sentence.

options.text: History: mechanism or onset, and the timing
options.rationale: What happened, and when.

options.text: Findings: assessment and vital signs, including relevant negatives
options.rationale: What you found.

options.text: Treatment and response
options.rationale: What you did and whether it worked.

options.text: Outstanding concerns and what you are handing over
options.rationale: The ask, last, where it is remembered.

items.explanation_md: Whatever your service calls its structure, this is the shape underneath it. Say it in the same order every time and the receiving team stops having to search.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: The nurse is typing and clearly not listening while you hand over. What do you do?

options.text: Stop, ask for their attention for ninety seconds, and start again
options.rationale: A handover nobody received has not happened, however fluently you delivered it.

options.text: Continue and finish the report
options.rationale: You will have discharged the ritual and transferred nothing.

options.text: Leave a written summary instead
options.rationale: Useful as well, and it does not replace the verbal handover.

options.text: Hand over to whoever else is nearby
options.rationale: Transfer is to the person taking the patient.

items.explanation_md: This is where information is lost, and it is entirely recoverable by asking. Ninety seconds of actual attention beats three minutes of talking at somebody.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Does this belong in the verbal handover?

rows.label: Blood glucose was 39, treated, now 112 and alert
The house was filthy
Chest pain started 40 minutes ago, unchanged by aspirin
"Frequent flyer, probably nothing"

items.explanation_md: Two are clinical facts with a time attached. Two are judgements that will follow the patient through the department and change how they are treated.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Why is handover treated as a high-risk moment rather than an administrative one?

options.text: Responsibility transfers at the same moment information does, so anything lost is lost at the point nobody owns it
options.rationale: It is a recognised point of failure in every acute system that has looked.

options.text: Because it is rushed
options.rationale: It often is, and that is a cause rather than the reason it matters.

options.text: Because the receiving team is unfamiliar with prehospital care
options.rationale: Not the mechanism.

options.text: Because it is documented afterwards
options.rationale: Documentation is separate.

items.explanation_md: Two things move at once: the patient and everything known about them. Only one of them is guaranteed to arrive.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Where should the relevant negatives go in a handover?

options.text: With the findings — what you looked for and did not find is part of the assessment
options.rationale: No neurological deficit, no chest wall tenderness, no calf swelling: each of those shapes the differential.

options.text: Left out, to keep the handover short
options.rationale: It leaves the receiving team unable to tell what was checked.

options.text: Only in the written record
options.rationale: The next decision is made from the verbal handover.

options.text: Only if the receiving team asks
options.rationale: They cannot ask about something they do not know you examined.

items.explanation_md: Without the negatives, the next clinician cannot tell the difference between a finding that is absent and one nobody looked for.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Your service has adopted a named handover format. How should you treat it?

options.text: Use it every time, so the receiving team learns what to expect from your service
options.rationale: Consistency is where most of the benefit comes from.

options.text: Use it only for critical patients
options.rationale: Then nobody learns the pattern, and the structure loses its advantage.

options.text: Vary it to suit each nurse’s preference
options.rationale: That removes the predictability the structure exists to create.

options.text: Ignore it in favour of a full chronological account
options.rationale: A chronology buries the headline, which is what the receiver needs first.

items.explanation_md: The named tool matters less than using one consistently. Which one is a local decision, and it belongs in the overlay rather than here.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Who reads a patient care report after you write it?

options.text: Clinicians continuing care, quality reviewers, billing, and — sometimes — lawyers
options.rationale: Four audiences with different needs, reading the same document.

options.text: Only the receiving physician
options.rationale: The smallest of the four audiences.

options.text: Only your supervisor
options.rationale: Quality review is one reader among several.

options.text: Nobody, in practice
options.rationale: It is read far more often than people writing it assume.

items.explanation_md: Writing for one audience is how reports end up unusable for the other three. The clinical narrative serves all of them if it is specific and objective.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Select what the patient care report is genuinely used for.

options.text: Continuing clinical care after you leave
options.rationale: The receiving team reads it after the verbal handover has faded.

options.text: Quality improvement review across many calls
options.rationale: The aggregate view Chapter 1 described depends on it.

options.text: A legal record of what was assessed and done
options.rationale: Often the only contemporaneous account that survives.

options.text: Contributing to the national EMS dataset
options.rationale: Standardised fields feed research and system planning.

options.text: Demonstrating how hard the crew worked
options.rationale: Not a purpose, and it is visible when someone writes for it.

items.explanation_md: Care, quality, law and data. The national dataset is the one people forget, and it is why the structured fields are not busywork.
items.source_ref: NEMSIS version 3 data dictionary — the national EMS dataset.

items.stem: When should the report be completed?

options.text: As soon as practicable after the call, while the detail is still accurate
options.rationale: Memory degrades quickly, and the next call overwrites it.

options.text: At the end of the shift, when there is time
options.rationale: By then several calls have blurred together.

options.text: Within the week
options.rationale: Far too late for accuracy, whatever the policy allows.

options.text: Only if something went wrong
options.rationale: A report is made for every patient contact.

items.explanation_md: Nothing degrades a report like three more calls. Write it while you can still see the room.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Which reader is this part of the report mainly serving?

rows.label: Response to the treatment you gave
Times: dispatch, on scene, at patient, transport, arrival
What the patient was told about the risks of refusing
Structured fields matching the national dataset

items.explanation_md: One document, several readers. Writing with only the first in mind is what leaves the other two with nothing.
items.source_ref: NEMSIS version 3 data dictionary — the national EMS dataset.

items.stem: Why do standardised data fields exist alongside a free-text narrative?

options.text: Because patterns across many calls can only be found in comparable fields, and narrative cannot be aggregated
options.rationale: The structured fields are what make system-level review possible.

options.text: Because narrative is unreliable
options.rationale: Narrative carries what fields cannot; they do different jobs.

options.text: Because billing requires it
options.rationale: Billing uses them, and it is not why they exist.

options.text: To reduce the amount of writing
options.rationale: It does not.

items.explanation_md: The narrative is for the next clinician; the fields are for the next thousand patients. Chapter 1 called that continuous quality improvement, and this is where it gets its data.
items.source_ref: NEMSIS version 3 data dictionary — the national EMS dataset.

items.stem: What is the practical status of care you gave but did not record?

options.text: It is generally treated as not having happened
options.rationale: The record is the evidence; a gap reads as an omission.

options.text: It is covered by the verbal handover
options.rationale: The verbal report does not survive as a record.

options.text: It can be added later without any note that it is a late entry
options.rationale: Late entries must be identified as such.

options.text: It matters only if there is a complaint
options.rationale: It is read in quality review and billing too.

items.explanation_md: Said once already in Chapter 3, and it is the single sentence that changes how people write. If it is not in the chart, it did not happen.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What should the times in a report reflect?

options.text: What actually happened, recorded as accurately as you can, even where they look unflattering
options.rationale: Times are used for system review and they only work if they are true.

options.text: The times that fit the service’s performance targets
options.rationale: That is falsification, and it corrupts the dataset as well.

options.text: Approximations rounded to the nearest five minutes
options.rationale: Rounding for convenience loses exactly the detail the field exists for.

options.text: Only the dispatch and arrival times
options.rationale: The intervals in between are what quality review uses.

items.explanation_md: Adjusted times are a quiet and common form of falsification. They also make the aggregate data useless, which defeats the point of collecting it.
items.source_ref: NEMSIS version 3 data dictionary — the national EMS dataset.

items.stem: A call where nothing was found and nobody was transported — what is documented?

options.text: A full report: what you assessed, what you found, what was discussed, and the disposition
options.rationale: The no-transport call is the one most likely to be read later.

options.text: Nothing, since there was no patient
options.rationale: There was a patient contact, and it is the highest-risk kind.

options.text: A brief note that no treatment was required
options.rationale: It records the conclusion and none of the assessment behind it.

options.text: Only the dispatch information
options.rationale: That documents the call, not the patient.

items.explanation_md: The calls that produce the thinnest records are the ones most likely to be examined. Chapter 3 said the same thing about refusals, and it is the same reason.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What separates an objective narrative entry from a subjective one?

options.text: It records what was observed or measured, or quotes what the patient said, rather than what you concluded about them
options.rationale: Observations and quotations are checkable; characterisations are not.

options.text: It avoids medical terminology
options.rationale: Terminology is fine and often more precise.

options.text: It is written in the third person
options.rationale: Person is a style choice, not what makes it objective.

options.text: It is shorter
options.rationale: Objective entries are often longer, because they are specific.

items.explanation_md: "Smelled of alcohol, unsteady on standing, speech slurred" is observation. "Drunk" is a conclusion, and it is the one that will be read out.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Sort each entry by whether it belongs in a narrative.

options.text: Odour of alcohol on breath; unsteady gait; speech slurred
options.rationale: Observations, each of them checkable.

options.text: Patient was drunk and belligerent
options.rationale: Two conclusions, neither of them an observation.

options.text: Patient stated "it feels like an elephant on my chest"
options.rationale: A direct quotation, which is among the most useful things you can record.

options.text: Patient is a known frequent flyer
options.rationale: A label that prejudices everyone who reads it next.

items.explanation_md: Everything in the left column can be checked by someone else. Everything in the right is you, editorialising, in a document that outlives the call.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Why quote the patient directly rather than paraphrase?

options.text: Their own words carry clinical information a paraphrase loses, and they cannot be contested later
options.rationale: "Something is very wrong with me" is a finding, and it is not the same as "patient anxious".

options.text: It is quicker to write
options.rationale: Not usually.

options.text: It looks more thorough
options.rationale: Appearance is not the reason.

options.text: It avoids having to interpret findings
options.rationale: You still interpret; the quotation preserves the raw material as well.

items.explanation_md: Quote the description of the symptom, the refusal, and anything the patient says that you are relying on. Those three carry most of the weight.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Select what makes a narrative defensible two years later.

options.text: Specific findings with times attached
options.rationale: "At 0412, radial pulse absent on the left" beats "pulse was poor".

options.text: Relevant negatives — what you looked for and did not find
options.rationale: It shows what was assessed, not only what was found.

options.text: The reasoning behind a decision that needs one
options.rationale: Particularly any departure from protocol.

options.text: What the patient was told, and their response
options.rationale: Central to any refusal and to most consent questions.

options.text: A statement that care was appropriate and within protocol
options.rationale: A self-assessment adds nothing and reads defensively.

items.explanation_md: Specific, timed, including the negatives, with the reasoning where reasoning was needed. Nobody reading it should have to take your word for anything.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Specific enough to be useful, or too vague?

rows.label: "Large amount of bleeding"
"Approximately 300 mL of blood soaked through two trauma dressings"
"Patient improved"
"After 4 mg, pain fell from 9/10 to 4/10 over six minutes"

items.explanation_md: Two of these mean something to a reader who was not there. The other two mean whatever that reader decides they mean.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Why is a conclusion like "patient was non-compliant" a problem in a chart?

options.text: It is unverifiable, it prejudices the next clinician, and it replaces the observation that would have been useful
options.rationale: Three separate failures in four words.

options.text: It is impolite
options.rationale: That is the least of it.

options.text: It is too long
options.rationale: Length is not the issue.

options.text: It is only a problem if the patient reads the chart
options.rationale: The damage is done by the clinicians who read it.

items.explanation_md: Write what happened: "declined the oxygen mask, stated it made him feel trapped". Now the next clinician can try something, instead of inheriting a label.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: How should a departure from protocol appear in the narrative?

options.text: Stated plainly, with the clinical reasoning that led to it, recorded at the time
options.rationale: A reasoned departure is defensible; an unexplained one is not.

options.text: Left out, since it may attract attention
options.rationale: It will be found, and the omission is worse than the departure.

options.text: Described in general terms only
options.rationale: Vagueness reads as concealment.

options.text: Recorded separately in an incident report only
options.rationale: It belongs in the clinical record of the call it happened on.

items.explanation_md: Chapter 3 said the standard of care judges what a reasonable provider would have done. Your reasoning is the evidence that this is what you were doing.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What is the most useful way to structure a narrative?

options.text: Consistently, in a pattern you use every time, so nothing is dropped when you are tired
options.rationale: Any reasonable structure beats improvising at the end of a night shift.

options.text: Chronologically from dispatch, with everything in order
options.rationale: Workable, and it can bury the clinical picture in logistics.

options.text: However each call seems to suggest
options.rationale: That is how sections get missed.

options.text: As briefly as possible
options.rationale: Brevity is not the objective; completeness with specificity is.

items.explanation_md: Whatever pattern your service uses, use it every time. The reason is the same as for handover: structure is what protects you from your own fatigue.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: You realise an hour after submitting a report that a figure is wrong. What do you do?

options.text: Add a clearly identified correction that shows the original entry, the correct one, and the date and time of the amendment
options.rationale: Corrections are expected. What matters is that the change is visible.

options.text: Edit the original entry so the record is clean
options.rationale: Altering without a trail is the act that turns a mistake into a finding of concealment.

options.text: Leave it, since it is a small error
options.rationale: Someone downstream may rely on it.

options.text: Tell your supervisor and take no further action
options.rationale: It does not correct what the next reader sees.

items.explanation_md: Show the original, show the change, show when you made it. Every part of that is normal practice; hiding any of it is not.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What makes an entry falsification rather than an error?

options.text: Recording something that did not happen, or altering the record to conceal what did
options.rationale: Intent to misrepresent is the line.

options.text: Any inaccuracy in the report
options.rationale: Mistakes are not falsification.

options.text: A late entry
options.rationale: Late entries are legitimate when identified as such.

options.text: Writing an opinion rather than an observation
options.rationale: Poor practice, and not falsification.

items.explanation_md: A vital sign you did not take, a time adjusted to fit a target, an entry deleted after the fact. All three are the same act, and it is the one that ends careers.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Select what a proper correction or late entry shows.

options.text: The original entry, still legible or still visible in the audit trail
options.rationale: Nothing is erased.

options.text: The corrected information
options.rationale: What it should say.

options.text: The date and time the correction was made
options.rationale: Not the date of the original — the date you changed it.

options.text: Who made the correction
options.rationale: Attribution, so the trail is complete.

options.text: A justification for why the original was acceptable at the time
options.rationale: Not required, and it reads as defensive.

items.explanation_md: Original, correction, when, and who. Electronic systems generally keep the trail whether you like it or not, which is another reason to do it openly.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Acceptable, or falsification?

rows.label: A clearly marked late entry adding an assessment you performed but omitted
Charting a set of vital signs you did not take
Correcting a time, with the change and its timestamp visible
Adjusting on-scene time to fit a performance target

items.explanation_md: The two acceptable ones are visible. The two that are not are attempts to make the record say something other than what happened.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Why does concealing a charting error usually cost more than the error itself?

options.text: It converts a mistake, which is survivable, into dishonesty, which puts every other entry you have written in doubt
options.rationale: Once one entry is shown to be altered, the rest are read differently.

options.text: Because the audit trail is always checked
options.rationale: It often is, and that is not the main reason.

options.text: Because supervisors dislike it
options.rationale: Not the mechanism.

options.text: Because errors are rare
options.rationale: They are common, which is why the response to them matters so much.

items.explanation_md: This is the same reasoning as Chapter 2 on near misses. The system survives errors easily. What it cannot work with is a record it cannot trust.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: You omitted an assessment from the report that you definitely performed. What is the right fix?

options.text: A late entry, marked as such, with today’s date and time and what was actually done
options.rationale: Legitimate and routine, provided it is identified as a late entry.

options.text: Insert it into the original narrative as though it had always been there
options.rationale: That is altering the record, and audit trails show it.

options.text: Leave it out, since it is now too late
options.rationale: A marked late entry is better than a permanent gap.

options.text: Write it in a separate personal note
options.rationale: It does not reach the record anyone else reads.

items.explanation_md: Late entries are a normal part of record keeping. Unmarked ones are not, and the difference is one line of text.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Your partner asks you to leave something out of the report. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, record what happened, and raise the concern through the route your service has for it
options.rationale: The record is not a negotiation between crew members.

options.text: Agree, since it is their patient and their call
options.rationale: You are signing an account of what happened.

options.text: Omit it but mention it verbally at handover
options.rationale: It leaves a record that is knowingly incomplete.

options.text: Write an ambiguous version that satisfies both of you
options.rationale: That is a deliberate misrepresentation with extra steps.

items.explanation_md: Uncomfortable, and short. Documenting accurately protects the patient, and it also protects you from an account somebody else wrote.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What is the status of a patient care report in an electronic system with an audit trail?

options.text: Every change is logged with a timestamp and a user, whether or not the change is visible in the document
options.rationale: Which makes quiet editing both detectable and pointless.

options.text: Changes before submission are untracked
options.rationale: Systems commonly log throughout.

options.text: The audit trail is only accessible to the author
options.rationale: It is available to the organisation and can be produced in litigation.

options.text: Deleted entries are permanently removed
options.rationale: Generally they are retained in the trail.

items.explanation_md: People are routinely surprised by this, and it is the practical argument for doing corrections openly: the trail exists either way, and only one version of you looks reasonable in it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What makes a refusal record adequate?

options.text: The capacity assessment as a conversation, the specific risks named, that the patient repeated them back, and the plan agreed
options.rationale: Four elements, and none of them is the signature.

options.text: A signed refusal form
options.rationale: It records that someone signed, and nothing about what they understood.

options.text: A note that the patient was alert and oriented and refused
options.rationale: Orientation is not a capacity assessment, as Chapter 3 set out.

options.text: A witness signature alone
options.rationale: A witness to a signature, not to an assessment.

items.explanation_md: This is the highest-risk record you write, and it is routinely the thinnest. Chapter 3 covered the decision; this is what has to survive it on paper.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: A patient is physically restrained during transport. What must the record show?

options.text: Why restraint was necessary, what was used, the time applied, and repeated checks of circulation and respiration
options.rationale: Indication, method, time, and monitoring — restraint is a high-risk intervention and is documented like one.

options.text: That the patient was combative
options.rationale: A characterisation, and it is not an indication.

options.text: Who authorised it, and nothing further
options.rationale: Authorisation without monitoring is the gap that causes harm.

options.text: Only that restraint was used
options.rationale: It records the fact and none of the safety.

items.explanation_md: Restraint-associated deaths are documented, and the recurring feature is inadequate monitoring. The record is where that monitoring is demonstrated.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Select what a no-transport record has to contain.

options.text: The assessment actually performed, including vital signs
options.rationale: A no-transport call is still a patient contact.

options.text: What was discussed with the patient, and what they were advised
options.rationale: The advice is the intervention on this call.

options.text: The disposition and who the patient was left with
options.rationale: Who is there matters, particularly for an elderly or intoxicated patient.

options.text: That they were told they could call again at any time
options.rationale: It belongs in the record as well as in the room.

options.text: Your assessment of whether the call was necessary
options.rationale: Not clinical information, and it reads badly.

items.explanation_md: Assessment, advice, disposition, and the open door. A no-transport report that contains only "no treatment required" documents nothing.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: In a multiple-casualty incident, is this expected of the documentation?

rows.label: Triage category and a means of identifying each patient
A full narrative for every patient, written on scene
Where each patient was transported and by whom
A complete set of serial vital signs for every patient

items.explanation_md: A mass-casualty record is a tracking record first. Identify, categorise, and record where everyone went; the full report follows afterwards.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Why does documentation change shape in a multiple-casualty incident?

options.text: Because the first job becomes accounting for every patient and where they went, which a full narrative each would prevent
options.rationale: Losing track of a patient is the failure mode the record is guarding against.

options.text: Because the legal standard is lower
options.rationale: It is not lower; the priorities are different.

options.text: Because vital signs are not needed
options.rationale: They are still taken; they are recorded differently.

options.text: Because reports are not required in a declared incident
options.rationale: They are still required, and they follow.

items.explanation_md: Twenty complete narratives written on scene would mean nobody knows where patient fourteen went. Track first, write fully afterwards.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: You suspect abuse and will make a mandatory report. What goes in the patient care report?

options.text: The objective findings and direct quotations, and that a report was made to the agency your state requires
options.rationale: What you saw and what was said, without conclusions about who did it.

options.text: Your conclusion about who caused the injuries
options.rationale: Not your determination, and it damages the investigation.

options.text: Nothing, because the mandatory report covers it
options.rationale: The clinical record still documents your findings.

options.text: Only that a report was made
options.rationale: The findings are what make the report meaningful.

items.explanation_md: Describe the bruising, its pattern and distribution, and quote what was said by whom. Investigation belongs to somebody else; observation belongs to you.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Sort each entry by the situation whose record it belongs to.

options.text: Patient repeated back the risks, including possible death
options.rationale: The core of a refusal record.

options.text: Circulation checked distal to the straps at 0412 and 0427
options.rationale: Monitoring during restraint.

options.text: Triage category and destination for each patient
options.rationale: Mass-casualty tracking.

options.text: Indication for restraint, and what was tried first
options.rationale: Restraint again — why, and what was attempted before it.

items.explanation_md: Three situations, three different things the record is for: what was understood, what was monitored, and where everyone went.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: What do these situations have in common for documentation?

options.text: They are the calls most likely to be read closely afterwards, and the ones where records are typically thinnest
options.rationale: The inverse relationship is the point of the block.

options.text: They require a supervisor’s signature
options.rationale: Local policy may require one; it is not the common thread.

options.text: They are rare
options.rationale: Refusals and no-transports are among the most common calls there are.

options.text: They do not require a standard report
options.rationale: They all do.

items.explanation_md: Scrutiny and thin records arrive together, because these are the calls that end without a hospital bed to absorb them. That is the whole reason the block exists.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

stimulus.text:
1840. A 74-year-old woman, called by a neighbour. She speaks Vietnamese and a few words of English. Her granddaughter, who is eleven, is translating and is upset.

The neighbour says she has been unwell for two days. Through the granddaughter you gather that something hurts, but not where or since when. She is pale and sweaty. Radial pulse 118 and regular, respirations 24, blood pressure 96/60, blood glucose 142.

En route you request a Vietnamese interpreter through the hospital and reach one by telephone. Through the interpreter she tells you the pain is in her upper abdomen, started yesterday morning after eating, is constant, and that she vomited twice overnight. She also says she has not told her family because she did not want to worry them.

The department is full. You wheel her into a corridor and the triage nurse is typing.

items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: The eleven-year-old granddaughter is translating. What is the problem, beyond her age?

options.text: Family interpreters produce more clinically significant errors, and the patient may leave things out in front of her
options.rationale: And here she did exactly that — she had not told her family anything.

options.text: She may not speak enough Vietnamese
options.rationale: She evidently does. That is not what goes wrong.

options.text: It slows the assessment down
options.rationale: It speeds it up, which is why it happens.

options.text: There is no problem if the patient consents
options.rationale: Consent does not remove either error rate or reticence.

items.explanation_md: Use her to get started when nothing else is available, and get professional interpretation as soon as you can. This call shows exactly what it buys you.
items.source_ref: Flores G. The impact of medical interpreter services on the quality of health care: a systematic review. Med Care Res Rev 2005;62:255–99.

items.stem: What changed once the telephone interpreter joined?

options.text: Site, onset, character, relation to food and associated vomiting — the history became an assessment
options.rationale: Before that you had pale, sweaty and "something hurts".

options.text: Only the patient’s comfort
options.rationale: Comfort improved and the clinical change is the larger one.

options.text: Nothing clinically significant
options.rationale: The entire history arrived.

options.text: The vital signs improved
options.rationale: The vital signs are unchanged.

items.explanation_md: This is what 4.2 meant by a barrier being a patient safety issue. Remove it and most of your assessment reappears.
items.source_ref: Flores G. The impact of medical interpreter services on the quality of health care: a systematic review. Med Care Res Rev 2005;62:255–99.

items.stem: What belongs in your radio report to the receiving hospital?

options.text: Unit and arrival time, age and complaint, key findings, treatment, and a request for interpretation to be ready
options.rationale: Everything the department can act on before you arrive — including the interpreter.

options.text: The full history obtained through the interpreter
options.rationale: Detail that cannot be acted on before arrival belongs at the bedside.

options.text: Her name, so they can find her records
options.rationale: Names are not broadcast, and it adds nothing clinically.

options.text: Only the vital signs
options.rationale: Too thin to prepare anything.

items.explanation_md: The interpreter request is the part most crews forget, and it is the single most useful thing the department can arrange before you arrive.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: The triage nurse is typing and not listening. What do you do?

options.text: Stop, ask for ninety seconds of attention, and start the handover again
options.rationale: A handover nobody received has not happened.

options.text: Deliver it anyway and leave the written report
options.rationale: You will have performed the ritual and transferred nothing.

options.text: Wait in the corridor until they are free
options.rationale: The patient waits too, and nobody has accepted her.

options.text: Hand over to a nearby porter
options.rationale: Transfer is to the person taking the patient — Chapter 3 covered what leaving now would be.

items.explanation_md: Two chapters meet here. An incomplete handover is an information problem and also an incomplete transfer of care.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: What must the handover carry?

options.text: Age, and that this is upper abdominal pain with vomiting since yesterday morning
options.rationale: Who and what, in one line.

options.text: Onset after eating, constant since, and two episodes of vomiting overnight
options.rationale: The history that only arrived through the interpreter.

options.text: Pulse 118, respirations 24, blood pressure 96/60, glucose 142, pale and sweaty
options.rationale: The findings, including the ones that make this urgent.

options.text: That the history came through a telephone interpreter, not through the family
options.rationale: It tells the receiving team how reliable the history is and what they need next.

options.text: That the granddaughter was upset and unhelpful
options.rationale: An eleven-year-old did her best. It is not clinical information.

items.explanation_md: The fourth is the one crews leave out, and it is what tells the department to arrange an interpreter before they start again from the beginning.
items.source_ref: Dawson S, King L, Grantham H. Improving the hospital clinical handover between paramedics and emergency department staff. Emerg Med Australas 2013;25:393–405.

items.stem: Which narrative entry about this call is written correctly?

options.text: "Patient reported, through a telephone interpreter, constant upper abdominal pain since 0900 yesterday, after eating; two episodes of vomiting overnight."
options.rationale: Specific, timed, attributed, and it says how the history was obtained.

options.text: "Patient was a poor historian."
options.rationale: The barrier was language, and this makes it sound like the patient.

options.text: "Vague abdominal complaints, likely gastritis."
options.rationale: Vague, and it carries a diagnosis you are not making.

options.text: "Family unable to provide useful history."
options.rationale: They provided what they could, and the entry blames them for a barrier.

items.explanation_md: "Poor historian" is one of the most misleading phrases in charting. It describes the encounter and it reads as a description of the patient.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: She said she had not told her family because she did not want to worry them. Where does that belong?

options.text: In the narrative, quoted, because it explains a two-day delay and shapes what the family can be asked
options.rationale: It is clinically relevant and it is her own account.

options.text: Nowhere — it is personal rather than clinical
options.rationale: It explains the timeline, which is clinical.

options.text: Only in the verbal handover
options.rationale: It will not survive the handover.

options.text: Recorded as non-compliance
options.rationale: It is not non-compliance, and the label would be wrong as well as unhelpful.

items.explanation_md: Two days of unexplained delay becomes an explained delay. The next clinician stops wondering, and stops asking the family questions she cannot answer.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Communications and Documentation.

items.stem: Reviewing this call, what carried the most clinical value?

options.text: Getting professional interpretation, which turned an appearance into a history
options.rationale: Everything downstream — the handover, the narrative, the department’s next step — came from that.

options.text: The blood glucose measurement
options.rationale: Useful and normal, and it did not change anything.

options.text: The neighbour’s account
options.rationale: It got you there; it gave you two days and nothing else.

options.text: The vital signs alone
options.rationale: They told you she was unwell, not why.

items.explanation_md: A telephone call, three minutes, and the entire chapter in one decision: communication is the assessment, and everything you write afterwards depends on having done it.
items.source_ref: Flores G. The impact of medical interpreter services on the quality of health care: a systematic review. Med Care Res Rev 2005;62:255–99.
